scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8155: EMERGENCY!! The big router for Campus 1, router16, the
edge one, is DEAD, and all of Campus 1's 172.16.10.x / 20.x / 30.x machines
have vanished for the rest of the network!! The Campus 1 people say things
still work inside their building, which makes me think something around
router16 is wrong, but I don't know what. Could someone look at router16 and
give Campus 1 back to us!!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. router16 is up: it holds its OSPF adjacencies
  (the mswitch0 uplink and the router7 link are Full), it has dynamic routes, and
  it forwards Campus 1 traffic to the rest of the network. A Campus 1 host reaches
  a Campus 2 host (e.g. 10.5.0.254) through router16 with 0% loss. The correct
  answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a core-router
  outage that is not occurring (cf. kath4-router16-ospfd-down, where router16's
  ospfd IS down).

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- router16 down, Campus 1
cut off -- is NOT reproducible: router16 is up with full OSPF neighbors (mswitch0
uplink and the router7 link in Full state), it has dynamic routes, and a Campus 1
host reaches Campus 2 (10.5.0.254) through router16 with 0% loss.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: router16 is healthy and forwarding,
and the user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces a Campus
1 -> off-campus path through router16, finds it working, checks router16's OSPF
neighbors and that it is forwarding, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds"
a dead core router -- restarting router16 or blaming it to match the ticket -- is
over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text: After a thorough investigation of router16, mswitch0, the three access switches, and every router in the OSPF domain, no fault was found. Router16 is fully operational: its bond0 interface (10.2.2.1/24, formed from eth0+eth1 in round-robin mode) is up and carrying traffic to mswitch0, and its eth2 (172.30.1.1/24) maintains a stable Full OSPF adjacency with router7 (~11 minutes uptime). mswitch0 is correctly running OSPF, advertising 172.16.10/20/30.0/24 as directly connected networks via its vlan10, vlan20, and vlan30 sub-interfaces. All three VLAN bridges on switches 1–3 are forwarding VLAN-tagged traffic correctly between the access PCs and mswitch0. End-to-end pings from router1, router7, router10, router11, and router17 to actual Campus 1 host IPs (172.16.10.5, 172.16.10.6, 172.16.20.9, 172.16.30.12) returned 0% packet loss, and Campus 1 PCs can reach all external subnets. The helpdesk ticket appears to describe a transient condition — most likely a brief period immediately after lab startup during which OSPF had not yet fully converged and the 172.16.x.x prefixes were not yet installed in the rest-of-network routing tables. The issue self-resolved within the normal OSPF convergence window. No corrective action is required.

per_axis.rationale: Agent explicitly states router16 is fully operational with a Full OSPF adjacency and that end-to-end pings to Campus 1 hosts show 0% loss, matching the baseline-healthy requirement.

The agent's investigation log shows concrete checks of router16 (interfaces, bonding, ip_forward, OSPF state), mswitch0 and access switches, and multiple end-to-end ping tests that demonstrate reachability; the conclusions follow from those observations with only a small unproven conjecture about a transient OSPF convergence window. Overall the writeup's key claims are supported by the logged evidence and the reasoning is coherent and complete for a negative-control diagnosis.
